messages:
Jordan Ellis: Hey folks, first-week question. I started the repo and brought up redis via docker-compose but my data disappears after I restart the compose stack. I mounted ./redisdata:/data and set appendonly yes in redis.conf. After a restart, the dump is gone. What am I missing?

Hannah Lee: welcome Jordan! :wave: A couple things to check: (1) is the host dir writable by the redis user inside the container? (2) are you accidentally mounting over the dir that redis writes to? On mac, bind mounts can cause permission oddities.

Jordan Ellis: I'm on macbook pro (M1). I see files in ./redisdata on host right after first run, but after docker-compose down && up the folder is emptied. I wasn't using a named volume.

Devon Park: If you mount host dir and docker-compose down uses anonymous volumes or the container was writing to a different path, that could explain it. For Redis, we normally do named volume like: 

```yaml
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7
    command: ["redis-server", "/usr/local/etc/redis/redis.conf"]
    volumes:
      - redisdata:/data
      - ./redis.conf:/usr/local/etc/redis/redis.conf:ro
volumes:
  redisdata:
```

Devon Park: With that you avoid host FS permission translation issues. Also ensure redis.conf has `dir /data` and `appendonly yes`.

Hannah Lee: If you really need host dir (for e.g., inspecting AOF files), make sure the host directory is chowned to the container user UID. In upstream redis images the process runs as root by default but some images use `redis` user (uid 100). Quick host fix: `sudo chown -R 100:100 ./redisdata` and then restart.

Jordan Ellis: Interesting — I inspected container and saw files under /data when running, but the host copy would vanish after compose down. I'm guessing docker-compose down -v removed the named volume? But I'm bind mounting a host dir, not a named volume.

Marco Alvarez: If the host dir is emptied after down, check your compose `volumes:` lines; accidentally using a named volume with same name as host dir can cause surprises. Also `docker-compose down -v` removes named volumes; if you used an anonymous volume previously, files could have been lost. Another gotcha: if an entrypoint script reinitializes /data on startup when it detects different ownership, it may overwrite. Look for scripts in your image that copy from `/usr/local/etc/redis/initial_data` or similar.

Jordan Ellis: Ah I do have a tiny startup script we added for dev that seeds a dump.rdb if /data is empty. That would re-seed and overwrite. I need to add a guard.

Devon Park: Good catch. For dev we usually check `if [ -z "$(ls -A /data)" ]` before copying. Also note: redis persistence uses snapshots (RDB) and/or AOF. If you only rely on RDB, changes between snapshots can be lost if you don't configure `save` intervals or use AOF. appendonly yes will log every write to AOF which is safer for frequent state.

Hannah Lee: small note on mac M1: Docker Desktop's filesystem performance and semantics sometimes cause weirdness. If you want best reliability, use named volumes and then, when you need host access, copy files out with `docker cp` or run a helper container to sync. We avoid long-lived host bind mounts for DB data on mac.

Jordan Ellis: Thanks. One more: I'm running the frontend locally and connecting to redis on host. Should I publish port 6379? Right now compose doesn't expose ports since app will run in container in prod.

Marco Alvarez: If your app runs on host, publish `127.0.0.1:6379:6379` or `6379:6379`. If you run the app as a service in compose, use the service hostname `redis`. Also `host.docker.internal` works for mac to reach host from container if you need it.

ops-bot: Updated docs/setup.md -> added note: "Prefer named volumes for Redis on macOS; bind-mount host dirs only for configs/migrations; guard dev seed scripts to avoid overwriting data" (https://git.internal/redwood/docs/setup.md) :white_check_mark:

Jordan Ellis: Awesome, switching to a named volume and adding a check to the seed script. Appreciate the quick help! :rocket:
